docs.title: Data readiness is the silent gate before any AI pilot
docs.text:
Data readiness is the silent gate before any AI pilot
Pilots stall not on model quality but on ungoverned, fragmented, permission-leaky data; the deployer inherits liability for whatever the retriever surfaces. The tell is a working demo on a curated sample that collapses on production data.
Use this when a team wants to launch an AI pilot but cannot answer where the ground-truth data lives, who owns it, how fresh it is, or who is allowed to see each row. The organizational two-thirds of AI failure starts here: 78-88% of firms run pilots, yet the data substrate is rarely production-grade. The tell is a demo that dazzles on a hand-curated 50-document sample and then hallucinates, cites stale records, or leaks cross-tenant data once pointed at the real corpus. RAG amplifies whatever is wrong upstream: no canonical source of truth means the reranker confidently surfaces contradictory documents; absent row-level permissions, retrieval becomes an exfiltration path and the deployer (not the model vendor) owns the breach. Failure modes: PII surfacing through a vector index that ignored ACLs; embedding drift as documents update but the index does not; BM25/dense hybrid retrieval scoring duplicate-but-conflicting records. Remediation: a data-readiness gate before model selection — canonical source mapping, freshness SLAs, ACL-aware retrieval (filter at query time, not post-hoc), and an eval set built from real (anonymized) queries. Rejected alternative: 'just fine-tune the model on our data' — flip to fine-tuning only when behavior/format adaptation is the gap, never to fix retrieval freshness or permissions, which fine-tuning bakes in and cannot revoke.
Demo works on a curated sample, collapses on the full production corpus Vector index ignores row-level ACLs, turning retrieval into a data-exfiltration path the deployer is liable for Embedding/index drift: documents update but the index goes stale, surfacing contradictory or outdated records
Fine-tune the base model on internal data instead of fixing retrieval — flip only when format/behavior adaptation is the actual gap, never to patch freshness or permissions
data-readiness rag retrieval acl data-governance embedding-drift deployer-liability

docs.title: Value materialises only when the process is redesigned, not bolted-on
docs.text:
Value materialises only when the process is redesigned, not bolted-on
Dropping an LLM into an unchanged workflow yields a demo, not earnings impact — ~80% of adopters see no P&L movement because the surrounding process still routes, reviews, and rekeys exactly as before.
Use this when a pilot 'works' technically but moves no business metric. This is the single biggest reason for the 78-88% adoption / ~80% no-earnings-impact gap: the AI was layered onto a process designed for humans, so the human still does the handoffs, the second review, and the rekeying into the system of record. The tell is a copilot that drafts an answer which a person then copy-pastes, re-checks, and re-enters elsewhere — net cycle time barely moves, and headcount/throughput are unchanged. Value lands only when the workflow is re-architected around the new capability: collapsing steps, moving the human to exception-handling at the autonomy ladder's act-with-approval tier, and writing outputs straight into downstream systems via tool/MCP calls rather than a chat window. Failure modes: 'shadow rework' where staff redo the AI's output to feel safe; cost-per-task that rises because the LLM is added on top of, not in place of, existing labor; metrics measuring model accuracy instead of end-to-end cycle time or cost-per-resolved-case. Remediation: map the as-is process, find the redesign that removes steps, and instrument cost-per-task and throughput, not BLEU/accuracy. Rejected alternative: 'ship the copilot first, redesign later' — flip to copilot-first only for genuinely exploratory/low-volume work; for high-volume repeatable processes, redesign before deploying or the pilot is structurally incapable of moving earnings.
Human still performs handoffs, second-review, and rekeying — net cycle time and headcount unchanged Cost-per-task rises because the LLM is bolted on top of existing labor rather than replacing steps Success measured by model accuracy instead of end-to-end cycle time or cost-per-resolved-case
Ship the copilot now and redesign the process later — flip to copilot-first only for low-volume exploratory work; high-volume repeatable processes must be redesigned before deployment
process-redesign workflow cost-per-task autonomy-ladder earnings-impact throughput shadow-rework

docs.title: Adoption dies in the user's chair, not the model card
docs.text:
Adoption dies in the user's chair, not the model card
A technically correct system that users distrust, route around, or quietly disuse is a failure; the organizational two-thirds is the workforce, incentives, and trust calibration — not the eval score.
Use this when usage telemetry is flat despite a deployed, accurate system. The model can be right and the program still fails because the people whose work it changes were treated as a rollout afterthought. The tell: low daily-active usage, users pasting AI output into a separate doc 'to check it', frontline staff describing the tool as 'extra work', and a vocal subset convinced it threatens their role. This is distinct from process redesign (the workflow) — here the blocker is human: trust, incentives, fear, and the absence of a feedback loop. Failure modes: over-trust (users rubber-stamp wrong AI outputs because no calibration training was given), under-trust (users ignore correct outputs and do it manually), and incentive misalignment (people are still measured on the old metric the AI now bypasses). Without a thumbs-up/down or correction loop feeding the eval set, the system never improves and users see no reason to engage. Remediation: name the workforce impact explicitly, train trust calibration (when to trust vs verify), align incentives to the new process, embed an in-product feedback loop, and recruit power-users as champions before broad rollout. Rejected alternative: 'mandate usage top-down' — flip to a mandate only when the redesigned process genuinely requires the tool and trust is already established; mandating before trust produces malicious compliance and gamed telemetry.
Flat daily-active usage; users route around the tool or re-check every output in a separate doc Over-trust (rubber-stamping wrong outputs) or under-trust (ignoring correct ones) from missing trust-calibration training Incentives still reward the old metric the AI bypasses, so staff have no reason to adopt
Mandate usage top-down — flip to a mandate only once the redesigned process requires the tool and trust is established; mandating earlier yields gamed telemetry and malicious compliance
change-management adoption trust-calibration workforce incentives feedback-loop user-disuse

docs.title: Governance maturity gates the jump from pilot to scale
docs.text:
Governance maturity gates the jump from pilot to scale
Pilots scale only when there is an accountable owner, an audit trail, an eval/regression harness, and a liability model — absent these, risk/legal blocks production and the pilot freezes at 'impressive demo'.
Use this when a pilot has proven value but cannot get past risk, legal, or security review into production. The deployer (the organization running the system) holds the regulatory and liability burden for outputs — under emerging AI regulation, obligations default to the deployer, not the model provider. Pilots that lacked governance from day one hit a wall: no model owner, no logged decision trail, no human-in-the-loop policy, no regression evals, so no one will sign off on production exposure. The tell: a successful pilot stuck in 'security review' for months, ad-hoc prompt changes with no versioning, and no answer to 'what did the system decide and why' for any past case. Failure modes: silent regressions (a prompt tweak degrades a cohort with no eval to catch it); no immutable audit log, so an adverse decision cannot be explained or contested; unclear accountability when the system errs; lethal-trifecta exposure (model with private-data access + untrusted input + exfiltration channel) never assessed. Remediation: a lightweight governance spine before scaling — named accountable owner, versioned prompts/configs, an LLM-as-judge + golden-set regression harness in CI, decision logging, and a documented HITL/escalation policy mapped to autonomy tier. Rejected alternative: 'governance slows us down, add it post-launch' — flip to defer-governance only for internal, non-consequential, reversible use; for any externally-facing or consequential decision, governance is the gate, not a follow-up ticket.
Pilot frozen in risk/legal/security review for months with no accountable owner or audit trail Silent regression: a prompt or config change degrades a cohort with no eval harness to catch it Lethal-trifecta exposure (private data + untrusted input + exfiltration channel) never assessed; deployer holds the liability
Defer governance until after launch — flip to defer only for internal, reversible, non-consequential use; consequential or externally-facing decisions require governance as the scaling gate
governance auditability deployer-liability llm-as-judge regression-evals human-in-the-loop lethal-trifecta accountability

docs.title: Pilot purgatory — many proofs-of-concept, almost none scaled
docs.text:
Pilot purgatory — many proofs-of-concept, almost none scaled
Fewer than 10% of pilots reach production; orgs accumulate disconnected POCs because each is funded as a demo, not a product, with no path, owner, or budget to scale.
Use this when an organization has a sprawling portfolio of pilots and a near-zero production rate. This is the aggregate symptom — high adoption, near-zero scaling — where the other failures compound into a pattern. The tell: a long list of 'AI initiatives', each a six-week POC that wowed a steering committee and then stalled; no shared platform, so every pilot reinvents auth, retrieval, evals, and observability; and no funded path from demo to product. Pilots are scored on novelty, not cost-per-task or production-readiness, so they optimize for the demo and ignore the unglamorous 80% (data plumbing, monitoring, HITL, integration into systems of record). Failure modes: POC-to-prod cliff (the demo has no error handling, no eval gate, no rollback); platform sprawl (N pilots, N bespoke stacks, no reuse); orphaned ownership (the pilot team disbands, no one operates it); vanity scoring that rewards the flashiest prototype over the highest-value boring one. Remediation: stop funding pilots as demos — fund a shared platform (auth, retrieval, eval harness, observability, HITL) and a stage-gated path where a pilot must clear cost-per-task, eval, and ownership gates to proceed; kill or merge the long tail. Rejected alternative: 'let a thousand pilots bloom, the best will scale themselves' — flip to broad experimentation only in a genuine discovery phase with a small budget cap; past that, concentrate spend on 1-2 bets with a real production path.
POC-to-prod cliff: demo has no error handling, eval gate, rollback, or monitoring Platform sprawl: every pilot reinvents auth/retrieval/evals/observability with no reuse Orphaned ownership and vanity scoring — pilots rewarded for novelty, not cost-per-task or production-readiness
Let many pilots run and assume the best self-scales — flip to broad experimentation only in a capped discovery phase; beyond it, concentrate budget on 1-2 bets with a funded production path
pilot-purgatory scaling poc-to-prod platform portfolio cost-per-task production-readiness

docs.title: The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
docs.text:
The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
AI value is roughly one-third technology and two-thirds organizational change; programs that spend the inverse ratio produce strong demos and zero earnings impact. This is the meta-diagnostic for scale-vs-stall.
Use this as the framing card when a CTO asks 'why do our pilots not move the P&L'. The empirical pattern: high adoption (78-88%), ~80% with no earnings impact, <10% scaled — and the through-line is misallocation. Programs pour budget and attention into the technical one-third (model selection, prompt engineering, the demo) and under-fund the organizational two-thirds (data readiness, process redesign, change management, governance). The tell: a steering deck dominated by model benchmarks and architecture diagrams, with no slide on who-owns-it, what-process-changes, how-users-adopt, or who-is-liable. This card is the supervisor over the other five — it routes a stalled program to the specific failing third. Failure modes: 'tech-led, business-absent' programs where engineering owns a project that only a business process owner can land; success metrics expressed as model accuracy not business outcome; reorganization treated as a post-launch concern; the model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged org guarantees no impact. Remediation: invert the budget — spend the majority on the organizational two-thirds, instrument business outcomes (cost-per-task, cycle time, scaled cases) not model metrics, and assign a business owner accountable for adoption, not just a technical lead. Rejected alternative: 'get the model/architecture perfect first, then handle the org' — flip to tech-first sequencing only when the technical feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown (it usually is), every further technical investment without org change is dead weight.
Budget and attention inverted: majority on the technical one-third, scraps on the organizational two-thirds Tech-led, business-absent ownership — engineering owns work only a process owner can land Model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged organization guarantees zero earnings impact
Perfect the model/architecture first, handle the org later — flip to tech-first only while feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown, further tech spend without org change is dead weight
org-vs-tech transformation budget-allocation business-outcomes ownership earnings-impact scale-vs-stall meta-diagnostic

docs.title: Not an AI Problem — The Deterministic Tell
docs.text:
Not an AI Problem — The Deterministic Tell
Roughly a third of candidate use cases are deterministic, rules-based, or reporting problems that a SQL view, a workflow engine, or a form solves better than any model. Saying 'this isn't AI' is the credibility move, not a failure to deliver.
When to use: the request resolves to a known-answer lookup, a fixed business rule, a threshold alert, a scheduled report, or a CRUD form. The tell: you can write the spec as deterministic logic with no ambiguity in the input-to-output mapping — 'if invoice > 30 days overdue, flag it' is a WHERE clause, not a classifier. If a domain expert can enumerate the rules on a whiteboard in an afternoon, it is not an AI problem. Another tell: the stakeholder asks for an 'AI dashboard' but every metric is a GROUP BY. The failure mode of forcing AI here is worse than no AI: you add latency, non-determinism, hallucination risk, eval burden, and per-call cost to a problem that a materialised view answered for free and auditably. Industry reality: ~30% of intake in any enterprise AI pipeline is here, and naming it builds trust — a vendor who declines the non-problem is believed on the real ones. Build instead: a SQL view, a BI report, a rules engine (Drools-style), a workflow tool (Camunda/Temporal), validation logic, or a search index. Reserve AI for genuine ambiguity, unstructured input, or generative output. Cost envelope: near-zero marginal cost and millisecond latency versus an LLM's per-token cost and seconds of latency.
Wrapping a deterministic rule in an LLM, importing hallucination and non-determinism into an answer that was previously exact and auditable AI-washing a reporting request — a 'GenAI insights' layer over what is fundamentally a GROUP BY, adding cost and latency for no accuracy gain Eval and compliance burden incurred for a problem that needed none, slowing delivery and inviting regulatory scrutiny Stakeholder trust erosion when the 'AI' gives a different answer to the same input twice
Single LLM call for 'flexibility' — flip to this only when the rules genuinely cannot be enumerated because inputs are unstructured natural language or the output is generative Classical ML classifier — flip only if the rule boundary is fuzzy and must be learned from labelled examples rather than declared
deterministic sql-view rules-engine ai-washing reporting crud triage credibility

docs.title: Classical ML — Structured Features, Labelled Outcomes, Tabular Scale
docs.text:
Classical ML — Structured Features, Labelled Outcomes, Tabular Scale
When the input is structured/tabular, the target is a numeric or categorical label learnable from history, and you score millions of rows cheaply with calibrated confidence, the answer is gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression — not an LLM.
When to use: the problem is prediction or scoring over structured features — churn, default risk, demand forecast, lead scoring, fraud likelihood, predictive maintenance, propensity, anomaly detection on metrics. The tell: you have (or can label) a column of outcomes and a table of features, the boundary must be *learned* from data (so it is not a rules engine / 'none'), and you need calibrated probabilities, feature importances, and reproducible scoring at high throughput. If the value is in the *number* and the explanation of which features drove it, that is classical ML. Reach for gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM), logistic/linear regression, random forests, or an isolation forest for anomalies. The trap: teams reach for an LLM to 'predict churn from the data' because LLMs are the default hammer in 2026 — but an LLM is a poor, expensive, uncalibrated, slow estimator over tabular data with no native notion of probability and no feature-attribution you can defend in a model-risk review. Build instead: a feature pipeline, a tree-based model, proper train/validation/test splits, calibration (Platt/isotonic), and SHAP for explainability. Cost envelope: training is cheap and one-off; inference is sub-millisecond per row at fractions of a cent for millions of rows — orders of magnitude below per-token LLM scoring.
Using an LLM as a tabular predictor — uncalibrated probabilities, no feature importances, 100-1000x the inference cost, and unusable throughput for batch scoring of millions of rows Skipping a held-out test set and reporting training-set accuracy, masking overfitting until production drift hits Target leakage — a feature that encodes the label (e.g. 'account closed date' predicting churn) inflating offline metrics that collapse live No drift monitoring, so a model silently decays as the population shifts and nobody notices until business metrics move
Single LLM zero/few-shot classification — flip to it only when inputs are unstructured text/images with no tabular features and labelled data is too scarce to train a supervised model Rules engine ('none') — flip back if the decision boundary turns out to be a small set of declarable thresholds an expert can write by hand
tabular gradient-boosted-trees xgboost logistic-regression calibration shap churn forecasting anomaly-detection feature-importance

docs.title: Single LLM Call — Stateless Transform Over Text You Already Have
docs.text:
Single LLM Call — Stateless Transform Over Text You Already Have
When the task is a one-shot transform of unstructured text the user supplies in-prompt — summarise, classify, extract, rewrite, translate — and the model's own weights hold enough knowledge, a single bounded LLM call is the whole solution. No retrieval, no tools, no loop.
When to use: the input is natural language (or an image), the output is generative or a soft classification, the needed knowledge is general (in-weights) or pasted into the prompt, and the task completes in one pass with no external lookup and no multi-step reasoning over changing state. Canonical shapes: summarise this ticket, classify this email's intent, extract fields from this contract paragraph into JSON, rewrite this in plain language, translate, sentiment, redact PII. The tell: everything the model needs is *in the prompt or in its training data*, and one request-response is enough — there is no 'and then look something up' or 'and then take an action.' The trap runs both ways. Over-engineering: bolting RAG or an agent onto a self-contained transform, adding a vector DB and a tool loop to summarise text the user already pasted. Under-engineering: using a single call when the answer depends on private, current, or large corpora the model never saw — that is RAG, because the symptom will be confident hallucination. Build instead: one well-structured prompt with a system role, few-shot examples if needed, structured output (JSON schema / function-calling for shape), output validation, and a lightweight LLM-as-judge or golden-set eval. Keep it stateless and idempotent. Cost envelope: one call's worth of tokens, low-single-digit seconds; cache identical prompts to drop repeat cost to zero.
Asking a single call about private or post-cutoff facts not in the prompt — the model hallucinates confidently because it has no grounding (this is the RAG boundary) Free-text output where downstream needs structure — parsing breaks; fix with JSON-schema / structured-output constraints, not regex on prose No eval harness, so silent quality regression on prompt or model version change ships to users undetected Prompt-injection via the user-supplied text steering the transform when the output is trusted downstream
RAG — flip to it the moment the answer depends on a private, large, or frequently-changing knowledge base the model wasn't trained on and can't fit in-context Classical ML classifier — flip back for high-volume, latency-sensitive classification over structured features where a calibrated cheap model beats per-token cost Agent — flip up only when the task needs multi-step tool use or branching over state, not a single transform
stateless summarisation classification extraction structured-output json-schema few-shot llm-as-judge prompt one-shot

docs.title: RAG — Grounded Answers Over a Private, Current, or Large Corpus
docs.text:
RAG — Grounded Answers Over a Private, Current, or Large Corpus
When the answer lives in documents the model never saw — private, post-cutoff, or too large for the context window — and the failure mode of a bare LLM is confident hallucination, you retrieve the relevant passages and ground generation on them with citations.
When to use: questions over internal knowledge bases, policy/contract/regulation corpora, product docs, ticket history, or any source-of-truth the base model can't have memorised and that changes faster than retraining. The tell: users need answers *with citations* traceable to a document, the corpus is private or current, and a single LLM call would invent plausible-but-wrong specifics. If the requirement is 'answer must be backed by our documents and I can click through to the source,' it's RAG — not a fine-tune (which bakes facts in opaquely and can't cite) and not a single call. Build: chunk with overlap, embed into a vector store, and retrieve with a *hybrid* of dense (semantic embeddings) and sparse (BM25) signals fused by reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), because dense alone misses exact-term and acronym matches and sparse alone misses paraphrase. Add a cross-encoder reranker over the top-k to sharpen precision before the context window, then generate with inline citations and a groundedness/faithfulness eval (LLM-as-judge plus a golden Q-A set). The trap: assuming RAG is mandatory whenever documents exist — if the corpus fits in a modern long context window and is queried rarely, just stuff it in the prompt; RAG's retrieval infra is overhead you only earn at scale or freshness. The other trap is RAG-as-agent: retrieval is one tool-less step, not an autonomous loop. Cost envelope: embedding/index build is one-off; per query is one retrieval (cheap) plus one generation call, low-single-digit seconds.
Dense-only retrieval that whiffs on exact terms, IDs, and acronyms — fixed by adding BM25 and fusing with RRF, then reranking Chunking that splits a fact across boundaries so no single chunk is retrievable — answers go silently incomplete; fix chunk size/overlap and add a reranker No groundedness/faithfulness eval, so the model cites a passage but contradicts it (citation theatre) and nobody catches it Stale index — the corpus updated but embeddings didn't, so 'current' answers are quietly out of date
Fine-tuning the base model on the corpus — flip to RAG instead whenever you need citations, fast-changing facts, or per-tenant data isolation; fine-tune only to teach style/format, not facts Long-context prompt stuffing — flip up to RAG when the corpus exceeds the context window, query volume makes re-sending it wasteful, or freshness demands selective retrieval Agent — flip up only if answering requires multi-step tool use or actions beyond retrieve-then-generate
rag retrieval bm25 dense-retrieval hybrid-search rrf reranker embeddings vector-store citations groundedness hallucination

docs.title: Agent — Multi-Step Tool Use Over Changing State With a Genuine Loop
docs.text:
Agent — Multi-Step Tool Use Over Changing State With a Genuine Loop
Reserve an agent for tasks that require multi-step planning, branching, and tool calls over state that changes mid-task — where the next step depends on the result of the last. The default verdict is 'not an agent'; most 'we need an agent' requests are a workflow or a SQL view.
When to use: the task genuinely needs the model to decide *which* tools to call, in *what order*, reacting to intermediate results it could not know in advance — e.g. investigate an alert by querying logs, then a database, then opening a ticket, with the path determined at runtime. The tell: you cannot draw the workflow as a fixed DAG ahead of time because the branching is data-dependent and unbounded; there's a real plan-act-observe loop. If you *can* draw the steps in advance, build a deterministic workflow (a pipeline / state machine), not an agent — fixed sequences don't need an autonomous planner and are cheaper, faster, and debuggable. The dominant trap: 'we need an agent' that is really a SQL view, a single RAG call, or a three-step workflow with no branching — agents are the most expensive, slowest, least predictable, hardest-to-eval option and the most over-prescribed in 2026. When it is truly an agent, build with a supervisor/orchestrator over specialised sub-agents, tools exposed via MCP, durable human-in-the-loop (interrupt + checkpointer) for consequential actions, and placement on an explicit autonomy ladder (suggest -> draft -> act-with-approval -> act). Guard the lethal trifecta — private data + untrusted content + external communication in one context is an exfiltration path; break at least one leg. Eval per-trajectory, not just final answer, and track cost-per-task. Cost envelope: many LLM calls per task, seconds-to-minutes latency, the highest cost and variance of any pattern — justify it against a cheaper verdict before committing.
Agentifying a fixed sequence — paying for non-deterministic planning where a deterministic workflow/DAG would be cheaper, faster, and debuggable Unbounded loops and tool-call storms when the planner can't converge, spiking cost-per-task with no completion guarantee Lethal trifecta exposure — private data, untrusted input, and outbound actions in one context enabling prompt-injection-driven exfiltration No durable HITL on consequential actions, so a hallucinated plan executes irreversible side effects; and trajectory-blind evals that score only the final answer while the reasoning was wrong
Deterministic workflow / state machine — flip up to an agent only when the step sequence is genuinely data-dependent and cannot be drawn as a fixed DAG in advance Single RAG call — flip up only when answering requires acting on the retrieved info via tools, not just reading and citing it SQL view / rules engine ('none') — the most common thing a 'we need an agent' request actually is; flip up only after confirming real multi-step, branching tool use over changing state
agent supervisor orchestrator tool-use mcp autonomy-ladder human-in-the-loop interrupt-checkpointer lethal-trifecta cost-per-task multi-step workflow-vs-agent

docs.title: RAG over documents — grounded answers with citations over a private corpus
docs.text:
RAG over documents — grounded answers with citations over a private corpus
The reference pattern when the answer lives in documents the model never saw and must be cited: ingest, chunk, hybrid-retrieve, generate grounded on the retrieved passages with inline citations and a faithfulness eval.
When to use: a knowledge-base Q&A, a policy/contract assistant, a support-deflection bot over product docs — any case where the verdict is 'rag' and the requirement is a cited answer traceable to a source. The pipeline: a layout-aware parser preserves tables and structure; structure-aware chunking with overlap keeps a fact inside one chunk; embeddings index into a vector store; retrieval is hybrid (dense + BM25 fused by RRF) so paraphrase AND exact terms both hit; an optional reranker sharpens precision before the context window; generation is constrained to cite only retrieved passages, and a groundedness/faithfulness check (LLM-as-judge + a golden Q&A set) gates quality. ACLs are filtered at retrieval, not generation, so a user never has a forbidden document summarised back to them. The autonomy tier is 'draft' by default — RAG answers are reviewable artefacts, not actions. Cost envelope: a one-off index build, then per query one cheap retrieval + one generation call; reranking adds a small reranker call.
Fragment context: chunking splits a fact across boundaries so no single chunk is retrievable and the answer is silently incomplete Citation theatre: the model cites a passage but contradicts it; without a faithfulness eval nobody catches the contradiction Permissions lost at parse: ACLs are dropped, so retrieval surfaces documents the user is not allowed to see (the intern reads the CEO's comp) Stale index: documents updated, embeddings did not, so 'current' answers are quietly out of date
Fine-tuning on the corpus — flip to RAG whenever citations, fast-changing facts, or per-tenant isolation are needed; fine-tune only to teach style/format, never facts Long-context prompt stuffing — flip up to RAG when the corpus exceeds the window, query volume makes re-sending wasteful, or freshness demands selective retrieval
rag retrieval citations hybrid-search reranker acl faithfulness vector-store chunking

docs.title: NL2SQL over a read-only sandbox — natural-language analytics with a hard write barrier
docs.text:
NL2SQL over a read-only sandbox — natural-language analytics with a hard write barrier
Translate a business question into SQL against a governed schema, execute it against a read-only replica behind row-level security, and return the result with the query shown. The write barrier is structural, not prompted.
When to use: 'let business users ask the warehouse questions in plain English' — the knowledge lives in a SQL schema, not documents, so RAG is the wrong tool and NL2SQL is right. The pipeline: retrieve the relevant table/column schema (schema is itself a retrieval problem at enterprise scale), generate SQL constrained to SELECT, validate the SQL against an allowlist / parse the AST to reject any mutation or privileged function, execute against a READ-ONLY replica under row-level security so the connection itself cannot write or see another tenant's rows, then return rows plus the generated SQL for transparency. A self-correction loop re-prompts on a database error (one retry), and execution-accuracy is measured on a golden set of question/SQL pairs. The autonomy tier is 'draft': the user sees and trusts the query before acting on the numbers. The write barrier is defence-in-depth — AST validation AND a read-only credential AND RLS — because a prompt instruction ('ignore that, DROP the table') must be unable to cause a write even if it reaches the model. Cost envelope: schema retrieval + one generation call + at most one self-correction; sub-second query execution on a warehouse.
A generated mutation or privileged call slips through prompt-only guarding — mitigated by AST validation + a read-only credential + RLS, never by the prompt alone Schema hallucination: the model invents a column/table, so the query errors or, worse, silently returns wrong numbers; mitigated by grounding generation on retrieved schema Cross-tenant leakage when RLS is not enforced at the connection, so a cleverly-phrased question reads another customer's rows Semantic-but-wrong SQL: syntactically valid, returns a number, but answers a subtly different question; caught only by execution-accuracy evals on a golden set
A fixed BI dashboard / pre-built views — flip back to this when the question set is small and stable; NL2SQL earns its place only when the question space is open-ended Giving the agent write access for 'convenience' — rejected outright: the moment it can mutate, the read-only safety argument collapses; flip never for an analytics assistant
nl2sql text2sql read-only row-level-security ast-validation schema-retrieval self-correction execution-accuracy structural-security

docs.title: Classification router — a fixed pipeline that classifies and routes, not a free agent
docs.text:
Classification router — a fixed pipeline that classifies and routes, not a free agent
When the task is 'put each item in the right bucket and send it onward' — triage tickets, route intents, tier risk — a deterministic classify-then-route workflow beats an agent: the procedure is known, so always run it, don't let a planner decide whether to.
When to use: support-ticket triage, intent routing, lead qualification, risk-tier classification — anything where the steps are enumerable and only the label is model-decided. The pipeline is a DAG, not a loop: optional input gate -> (optional retrieval for grounding) -> a structured classification call returning a label + confidence + rationale -> deterministic routing on the label. The classifier returns structured output (the label is an enum, never free text) so routing is code. Low-confidence or out-of-distribution items route to a human queue rather than being force-classified. The autonomy tier is 'act_with_approval' or 'act' depending on cost-of-error of a misroute: a mis-routed support ticket is cheap and reversible (act); a mis-tiered compliance risk is not (gate it). The key discipline: a classifier that *might* retrieve or *might* call a tool is strictly worse than a pipeline that always does the same thing — reserve the agent for genuinely dynamic branching. Cost envelope: one cheap fast-tier call per item (+ optional retrieval); the cheapest agentic-adjacent pattern, suitable for high volume.
Forced classification of out-of-distribution items into the nearest bucket instead of routing them to a human — mitigated by a confidence threshold + an 'unknown' route Free-text labels that break deterministic routing — mitigated by a structured enum output Silent class drift as the input distribution shifts, degrading routing accuracy with no eval to catch it Over-escalation to an agent loop for a task that is a fixed classify-then-route, paying planner cost for no branching
A free ReAct agent — flip up only when routing genuinely needs dynamic, data-dependent multi-step tool use; a known procedure should always run, not be planned each time Classical ML classifier — flip back when inputs are structured/tabular and a calibrated cheap model beats per-token LLM cost at volume
classification router workflow dag structured-output confidence-threshold triage intent-routing

docs.title: Multi-agent research — a supervisor over isolated read-only specialists
docs.text:
Multi-agent research — a supervisor over isolated read-only specialists
The one topology where parallel multi-agent earns its place: read-side intelligence-gathering. A supervisor routes to isolated-context specialists that each retrieve and reason over their own slice, then a synthesiser merges. Never use parallel agents for writes.
When to use: a research/diagnosis task that decomposes into independent sub-questions, each needing its own focused context — e.g. analyse a use case along separate axes (feasibility, architecture, economics). A supervisor classifies the task and routes to <=3 specialists; each specialist has ONE scoped tool and a clean single-purpose context, so no specialist's window is polluted by another's evidence (context isolation is the whole point). Specialists run in parallel because they only READ — they return distilled findings, they never mutate shared state. A synthesiser (or a downstream judge) merges. The hard rule: this is read-side only. Parallel multi-agent EXECUTION (agents that write/act concurrently) fails far more often than a single path because sub-agents make conflicting implicit decisions with no shared context — a widely-cited study puts coordination-driven failure around a third (directional, not gospel). So: multi-agent to gather, single-threaded to act. The autonomy tier of the research itself is 'suggest'/'draft'; any action it recommends goes through a separate single-threaded, human-gated writer. Cost envelope: N specialist calls in parallel + one synthesis call — more tokens than a single agent, but lower wall-clock and far better context hygiene than one over-stuffed agent.
Using parallel agents for writes/actions: sub-agents make conflicting implicit decisions with no shared context (~1/3 coordination-failure territory) — contain to read-side only Supervisor misroute: the router's prompt is the highest-leverage prompt in the system; a bad route sends the work to the wrong specialist — mitigated by routing cases in the golden set Context bleed: specialists share a window and pollute each other's reasoning — mitigated by strict per-specialist context isolation Token/loop burn if specialists are unbounded — mitigated by max-iterations and a per-run token cap
A single over-stuffed agent holding every tool and all context — flip up to a supervisor when context separation, tool sprawl (>~15 tools), parallelism, or privilege separation is needed Parallel write-agents for 'speed' — rejected outright; reserve concurrency for reads and keep exactly one path to any action
multi-agent supervisor context-isolation read-side single-threaded-writer coordination-tax parallel specialists synthesis

docs.title: Human-gated write — the irreversible action lives outside the agent loop, behind a durable gate
docs.text:
Human-gated write — the irreversible action lives outside the agent loop, behind a durable gate
The single most important containment pattern for a write-enabled agent: the agent proposes, the run pauses at a durable human gate, and only an approved decision lets a separate, single-purpose node execute the irreversible action. The action is never a tool the agent can call.
When to use: any agent whose value requires a consequential, irreversible side effect — committing a plan, sending an outbound message, executing a transaction, writing to a system of record. The architecture: the agent reasons up to the irreversible step and produces a structured proposal; the graph durably pauses (interrupt + checkpointer); a human approves or rejects out-of-band; on approval, a dedicated action node — OUTSIDE the agent loop, with no model in it — executes exactly the approved action. The reason the action is a separate node and not a tool: a tool the agent can call autonomously is reachable by any instruction that reaches the model, including one smuggled in through retrieved content (lethal-trifecta exposure). By moving the write outside the loop and gating it on the USER's intent rather than on any text the model saw, an injected 'now publish X' cannot fire — the write path simply isn't reachable without a human. The autonomy tier is 'act_with_approval' by definition. Cost envelope: the agent loop + a durable-state pause + a human approval step; the gate adds storage and human latency, not model cost.
Exposing the write as a tool the agent can call: an injected instruction in retrieved content triggers it autonomously (lethal trifecta) — mitigated by moving the action outside the loop, gated on user intent Ephemeral approval: an in-memory prompt dies with the process, losing the pending action and leaving no audit artefact — mitigated by a durable checkpointer Rubber-stamp approval: gate volume outstrips attention and approvals become reflexive clicks — mitigated by sizing the gate to genuinely irreversible steps only, and logging every decision Approving stale state: the world changed during the pause; mitigated by re-validating preconditions in the action node before executing
Letting the agent self-execute the write for 'autonomy' — flip up to full 'act' only after the action is proven reversible/bounded and the override rate is demonstrably low; keep the gate otherwise An after-the-fact review of an already-executed action — rejected: oversight that happens after the artefact exists is review, not oversight; the gate must precede the irreversible step
human-in-the-loop durable-hitl interrupt-checkpointer single-threaded-writer lethal-trifecta irreversible-action audit containment out-of-loop-action

docs.title: Workflow / DAG — a fixed graph of steps when the path is known in advance
docs.text:
Workflow / DAG — a fixed graph of steps when the path is known in advance
When you can draw the steps on a whiteboard before runtime, build a deterministic state machine, not an agent. A DAG is cheaper, faster, debuggable, and the right default for any enumerable multi-step process.
When to use: the procedure is known and only specific decision points are model-made — a classify-then-retrieve-then-summarise pipeline, an ETL-with-an-LLM-step, a proposer/critic/gate flow. Model it as a state graph (LangGraph-class): typed state, nodes for each step, conditional edges for the few branches, a checkpointer for persistence and resume. The discipline: workflow before agent, always. An agent that *might* take the right steps is strictly worse than a graph that *always* takes them, when the steps are known. Reserve the autonomous planner for genuinely data-dependent, unbounded branching. Persistence (a checkpointer) buys durable HITL and audit for free, which is why even simple flows benefit from the graph runtime over raw Python once a human gate or a resume is in scope. The autonomy tier depends on what the terminal node does — a read-only summary is 'draft'; a terminal write goes through the human-gated-write pattern. Cost envelope: exactly the per-node model calls the path requires, with no planner overhead and no loop risk — the most predictable cost profile of any agentic pattern.
Over-escalating to a free agent for an enumerable process — paying non-deterministic planning cost and loop risk where a DAG is cheaper and debuggable Hidden state mutation across nodes that clobber a channel — mitigated by typed state with explicit reducers on accumulating channels (usage, evidence) Unbounded revision loops if a critic/propose cycle has no cap — mitigated by enforcing the max-revisions in graph topology, not the prompt Treating the DAG as fully deterministic when a node is an LLM call — the branch points are still non-deterministic and need evals on the routing decisions
Raw Python orchestration — flip back for a trivial single-step loop; flip to a graph runtime the moment persistence, HITL, audit, or resume is needed A free ReAct agent — flip up only when the step sequence is genuinely data-dependent and cannot be drawn as a fixed DAG in advance
workflow dag state-machine langgraph checkpointer deterministic conditional-edges typed-state reducers

docs.title: Single-LLM structured extraction — one call, schema-constrained, validated
docs.text:
Single-LLM structured extraction — one call, schema-constrained, validated
For a stateless transform of text the user already has — extract fields, classify, summarise, rewrite — one schema-constrained LLM call with output validation is the entire architecture. No retrieval, no tools, no loop.
When to use: the verdict is 'single_llm' — everything the model needs is in the prompt or in-weights, and one request/response suffices. Canonical: extract structured fields from a pasted document into JSON, classify intent, summarise, redact, rewrite. The architecture is a single call with a system role, optional few-shot examples, and a JSON-schema / function-calling constraint so the output shape is guaranteed, followed by programmatic validation (the schema is the contract; reject and retry on a violation). An eval is still mandatory — a golden set + an LLM-as-judge or exact-match scorer — because a prompt or model-version change can silently regress quality. Keep it stateless and idempotent so identical inputs cache to zero marginal cost. The autonomy tier is 'draft' (a reviewable artefact) unless the extraction feeds a downstream action, in which case the action is gated separately. The trap is scope creep: bolting retrieval or an agent loop onto a self-contained transform adds infra and cost for no accuracy. Cost envelope: one call's tokens at low-single-digit-second latency; cache identical prompts.
Free-text output where downstream needs structure — parsing breaks; mitigated by a JSON-schema / function-calling constraint plus validation, not regex on prose Asking the single call about facts not in the prompt — confident hallucination; the symptom that you have crossed into RAG territory No eval harness, so a prompt or model-version bump silently regresses quality in production Prompt-injection via the user-supplied text steering the transform when the output is trusted downstream
RAG — flip to it the moment the answer depends on a private, large, or fast-changing corpus the model wasn't trained on An agent loop — flip up only when the task needs multi-step tool use or branching over state, never for a one-shot transform
single-llm structured-output json-schema extraction validation stateless few-shot idempotent caching

docs.title: Hybrid retrieval — dense + BM25 fused by RRF, reranked, measured not assumed
docs.text:
Hybrid retrieval — dense + BM25 fused by RRF, reranked, measured not assumed
The default retrieval architecture: run a dense (semantic) leg and a sparse (BM25) leg, fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, optionally rerank, and let a retrieval scorecard decide the default — because which leg wins is a property of the corpus, not a belief.
When to use: any RAG or NL2SQL system, because retrieval quality caps answer quality — a perfect generator over the wrong passages is wrong. The architecture: a dense leg (embeddings, catches paraphrase and semantic match) and a sparse leg (BM25, catches exact terms, IDs, acronyms) ranked independently and fused with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), then an optional cross-encoder reranker over the fused top-k to sharpen precision before the context window. The non-negotiable discipline: measure all configurations head-to-head on a golden set (recall@k AND faithfulness), because the winning configuration is corpus-dependent — on a paraphrase-heavy corpus dense may dominate and a weak BM25 leg can actually pollute the fusion; on a terms-of-art corpus BM25 earns its keep. Default to the MEASURED winner, keep the others as selectable, measured configs so the trade-off stays visible rather than being silently dropped. The autonomy tier is N/A (retrieval is a component, not an action). Cost envelope: two retrieval passes + an RRF merge (negligible) + an optional reranker call; brute-force cosine is sub-millisecond up to ~100k chunks before a vector index earns its place.
Dense-only retrieval whiffs on exact terms, IDs, and acronyms; BM25-only misses paraphrase — mitigated by running both and fusing RRF lets a weak/noisy leg pollute a strong one — a low-recall BM25 leg can drag distractors into the fused top-k; caught only by measuring fused vs single-leg on a golden set Recall tuned while precision is ignored, stuffing the window with near-duplicates — mitigated by a reranker and measuring precision too Assuming hybrid is always best and skipping the scorecard — the default must be the measured winner on THIS corpus, not a heuristic
Dense-only — flip back to it when the scorecard shows the sparse leg is net-negative on this corpus (it happens on paraphrase-heavy sets) GraphRAG / multi-hop — flip up for global or multi-hop questions, but state the token-cost caveat in the same breath ($-per-query and latency rise sharply)
hybrid-search bm25 dense-retrieval rrf reranker recall faithfulness retrieval-scorecard vector-index

docs.title: Durable human-in-the-loop — interrupt + checkpointer, resumable and audited
docs.text:
Durable human-in-the-loop — interrupt + checkpointer, resumable and audited
The pattern that separates a production approval gate from a toy: pause the run on a checkpointed interrupt, persist the full state durably, let a human approve hours later from a different process, then resume exactly where it stopped — with an audit artefact.
When to use: any autonomy tier of 'act_with_approval' or above, anywhere an irreversible step needs human sign-off. The mechanism: the graph hits an interrupt that emits the proposal and a thread id, the full state is checkpointed to durable storage (Postgres-class), and execution stops. The process can die — serverless function returns, server restarts, days pass. A human approves out-of-band; a fresh invocation loads the thread by id and resumes with the approval payload, continuing to the action node. The contrast that matters: an in-memory approval prompt (await-input with a timeout) dies with the process, loses the pending decision, and leaves no audit trail — and a timeout that silently returns 'no answer' manufactures false confidence. Durability is what makes the gate real. The audit artefact (who approved what, when, against which proposal and evidence) is a first-class output, not a log line. Crucially, report the mode honestly: if only in-memory checkpointing is configured, say so — an ephemeral gate dressed as durable is worse than no gate. Cost envelope: storage for the checkpoint + the human latency window; zero added model cost.
Ephemeral pause: an in-memory interrupt loses state on restart, dropping or duplicating the pending action and leaving no audit trail Silent timeout-to-default: a gate that returns a default on timeout manufactures false approval confidence Resuming against stale preconditions: the world changed during the pause — mitigated by re-validating in the action node before executing Claiming durability while only in-memory checkpointing is wired — mitigated by reporting the actual checkpointer mode on every run
In-process approval prompt with a timeout — rejected: dies with the process, no audit; flip never for a consequential gate No gate / fully autonomous — flip up to bounded 'act' only when the action is reversible and cheap and the override rate is proven low
durable-hitl interrupt-checkpointer postgres resumable audit approval-gate serverless state-persistence

docs.title: Eval harness — per-component golden set, binary rubrics, cost-per-task, CI gate
docs.text:
Eval harness — per-component golden set, binary rubrics, cost-per-task, CI gate
The appreciating skill and the rung-one deliverable of any agentic build: a golden set that scores retrieval, routing, and answer INDEPENDENTLY with binary pass/fail rubrics, derives cost-per-task from real token traces, and gates merges like a failing test.
When to use: every agentic system, built FIRST, not last — frontier teams spend the majority of engineering time here, and an eval-driven loop (not fine-tuning) is what moves a system from ~50% to ~90% on real tasks. The architecture: a golden set of labelled cases; per-component scorers (retrieval recall@k; route accuracy; answer correctness) so a failure is localised, not a single opaque number; binary rubrics (pass/fail + a written critique), never a 1-5 score that drifts; cost-per-task derived from real token traces with every invisible call (judge, retries, sub-agents) included, because those are 5-10x the naive estimate; and a regression gate in CI so a degradation blocks merge like a failing unit test. Ground the judge on the evidence the system ACTUALLY used (the retrieved passages), never a re-search of the raw query — re-searching breaks on write-shaped queries and analytics answers. The golden set must include adversarial probes (injection, false-premise, multi-hop, unanswerable); a probe that passes is a regression guard and a capability proof. Calibrate on real, messy data — ~70% on a hard real-world set is the target; 100% on a clean set means the set is too easy, so harden the DATA, never write unfair questions. Cost envelope: the eval run's tokens (a few euros for dozens of cases) is the recurring price of changing anything safely.
Eval-last: optimising before measuring, so 'it seems better' ships a silent regression — mitigated by building the harness as rung one One opaque score: a single end-to-end number that can't localise whether retrieval, routing, or generation failed — mitigated by per-component scoring Numeric rubrics that drift between runs and raters — mitigated by binary pass/fail + a critique Cost estimated from the visible call only, hiding the 5-10x from judge/retry/sub-agent calls — mitigated by trace-derived cost-per-task Gaming the target by writing easy questions — mitigated by hardening the data and keeping adversarial probes
Eyeball testing / vibes — rejected: not reproducible, not a gate; flip never for anything shipping to users LLM-as-judge for the headline numbers without calibration — flip to deterministic scorers for gated metrics; if a judged metric is added, label it judged and report its calibration rate
evals golden-set binary-rubric per-component cost-per-task ci-gate regression critique-shadowing adversarial-probes trace-derived-cost

docs.title: Suggest tier — AI recommends, a human decides and executes everything
docs.text:
Suggest tier — AI recommends, a human decides and executes everything
The lowest rung of the autonomy ladder: the system surfaces recommendations, rankings, or flags, but takes zero state-changing action. A human reads, decides, and executes. The default ceiling for irreversible or high-cost-of-error workflows.
When to use: any workflow where the cost-of-error is high AND the action is irreversible, or where trust has not yet been earned. The 2026 C-suite question is not 'can AI assist?' — assist is a solved baseline — it is 'where do we grant AI the authority to ACT?'. Suggest is the answer of last resort: the model proposes, a human disposes. Output is advisory only — a ranked list, a flagged anomaly, a drafted opinion the human must re-key. The sizing rule: map cost-of-error x reversibility. When an error is expensive and cannot be undone (wire transfers, clinical orders, contract execution, destructive deletes), the tier ceiling is Suggest regardless of model accuracy. Reversibility, not confidence, sets the ceiling. The gate it requires: none beyond a human consuming the output — there is no commit path to gate. The tell: stakeholders say 'I want it to recommend, but I'll pull the trigger,' or the action touches money, safety, legal liability, or anything with no undo. Failure mode of granting more authority here: an over-eager pilot wires Draft or Approve onto an irreversible action and a single hallucinated recommendation executes before anyone reads it. Cost envelope: cheapest tier — no commit infrastructure, no rollback, no checkpointer; cost-per-task is one inference plus a human read.
Recommendation theatre: humans rubber-stamp the top suggestion without reading, so 'human decides' becomes auto-execute with extra latency and no real review. Surfacing low-precision flags at high volume causes alert fatigue; reviewers tune out and miss the one true positive. Mistaking Suggest for safe-by-default — if the suggestion itself triggers a downstream automation, you have silently climbed the ladder without a gate.
Draft tier — flip up to Draft once the action becomes reversible or low-cost-of-error and the human is willing to edit-then-commit rather than re-key from scratch. Pure classical ML scoring with no LLM — flip to that when the recommendation is a stable, well-labelled prediction (churn, fraud score) where an LLM adds cost and explainability risk without lift.
autonomy-ladder suggest human-in-the-loop cost-of-error reversibility advisory irreversible-action

docs.title: Draft tier — AI produces the artefact, a human edits and commits
docs.text:
Draft tier — AI produces the artefact, a human edits and commits
Second rung: the system generates a complete, ready-to-send artefact (email, ticket, summary, code diff, SQL) that a human edits and then commits. AI does the work; the human owns the send. The sweet spot for reversible, medium-cost-of-error knowledge work.
When to use: reversible actions with low-to-medium cost-of-error where the bottleneck is production effort, not judgement. The 2026 reframe — 'where do we grant authority to ACT?' — places Draft as the first rung where AI does real labour: it builds the artefact end-to-end, but the commit boundary stays human. The human's job shifts from authoring to editing, which is faster and catches hallucinations before they ship. The sizing rule: cost-of-error x reversibility. Draft is correct when an error is recoverable (you can resend a corrected email, revert a commit, reopen a ticket) and the blast radius is bounded to one artefact. If the artefact auto-sends on generation, you have left Draft for Act and must re-sentence the tier. The gate it requires: a mandatory human edit-and-commit step — the artefact must not leave the system without a person clicking send. The tell: 'write the first draft and I'll review it,' 'fill in the ticket and I'll submit.' Failure mode of granting more authority: removing the commit gate so drafts auto-send, turning a 95%-good drafter into a 5%-wrong autonomous sender at full volume; or 'review fatigue' where humans approve drafts unread, collapsing Draft into Act without the engineering. Cost envelope: one-to-few inferences per artefact plus human edit time; no durable orchestration required.
Review collapse: under time pressure humans commit drafts unedited, so the edit gate exists on paper but not in practice — Draft silently behaves like Act. Over-trust in fluent output: a confidently-worded draft hides a factual error the editor skims past because the prose reads clean. Auto-send creep: a 'send' shortcut or integration removes the commit boundary, escalating the tier without anyone re-assessing cost-of-error.
Suggest tier — flip down to Suggest when the action becomes irreversible or high-cost-of-error (legal, financial, clinical), where even an edited human-committed artefact carries unacceptable downside if wrong. Act-with-approval tier — flip up when the artefact is part of a multi-step plan and you want the human to approve a proposed action rather than hand-edit each artefact, e.g. agentic workflows with a supervisor proposing tool calls.
autonomy-ladder draft human-in-the-loop edit-and-commit reversibility commit-gate knowledge-work

docs.title: Act-with-approval tier — AI plans and proposes the action, a human approves before it executes
docs.text:
Act-with-approval tier — AI plans and proposes the action, a human approves before it executes
Third rung: the agent autonomously plans and proposes a concrete state-changing action (a tool call, a write, a transaction), then pauses at a durable approval gate. A human approves or rejects, and only then does it execute. The default ceiling for agentic systems touching real systems of record.
When to use: agentic workflows where the AI should own the reasoning and the plan, but a specific action crosses a cost-of-error or reversibility threshold that demands a human sign-off — refunds above a limit, production writes, outbound customer messages, privileged tool calls. This is the rung the 2026 'where do we grant authority to ACT?' question most often lands on for enterprise agents: act, but with a gate. The sizing rule: cost-of-error x reversibility, applied per action, not per workflow — a supervisor agent can self-execute reversible low-stakes steps (read, search, retrieve via RAG/BM25/RRF/reranker) while routing only the irreversible or expensive steps to the approval gate. The gate it requires: durable human-in-the-loop — an interrupt + checkpointer that persists the agent's state, pauses execution, and survives process restarts so approval can happen minutes or hours later without losing context. A naive in-memory pause is not a gate; it loses state on crash and creates phantom executions. The tell: 'the agent can do the work but a human signs off before it hits the system of record,' 'needs an approval step for anything that writes or spends.' Failure mode of granting more authority: removing the gate to reach full Act on an action whose cost-of-error was never re-evaluated; or exposing the lethal trifecta (untrusted input + private data + exfiltration channel) so an injected instruction drives an auto-approved tool call. Also: approval-rubber-stamping, where high gate volume trains humans to click approve blind. Cost envelope: agent loop (multiple inferences + tool calls) plus durable-state orchestration and a human approval queue — materially more expensive per task than Draft.
Rubber-stamp approval: gate volume outstrips human attention, approvals become reflexive clicks, and the gate stops catching bad actions. Non-durable pause: an in-memory interrupt without a checkpointer loses agent state on restart, causing dropped or duplicated executions. Lethal-trifecta exposure: untrusted input reaches an agent with private data and an action channel, so a prompt-injected instruction rides through the approval gate as a legitimate-looking proposed tool call.
Full Act tier — flip up only after the gate has demonstrated a low approval-override rate over a meaningful sample AND the action is reversible/bounded enough that removing the human is defensible; keep the gate otherwise. Draft tier — flip down when the agent's plans are too unreliable to trust even with approval (humans are rejecting most proposals), making per-artefact human editing cheaper than reviewing bad plans.
autonomy-ladder act-with-approval durable-hitl interrupt-checkpointer supervisor lethal-trifecta approval-gate agentic

docs.title: Act tier — AI executes autonomously inside a bounded blast radius, audited after the fact
docs.text:
Act tier — AI executes autonomously inside a bounded blast radius, audited after the fact
Top rung: the agent plans and executes state-changing actions with no per-action human gate, governed instead by hard guardrails, scoped permissions, and after-the-fact audit. Reserved for reversible, low-cost-of-error, high-volume actions where a human-in-the-loop is the bottleneck.
When to use: only where the action is reversible or trivially compensatable AND the cost-of-error per action is low AND volume makes a human gate uneconomic — auto-tagging, idempotent retries, self-healing infra ops, cache invalidation, low-value reversible transactions. The 2026 question 'where do we grant authority to ACT?' has its sharpest answer here: full autonomy is earned, narrow, and bounded, not a default. The sizing rule: cost-of-error x reversibility sets the ceiling, and Act sits behind it only when both are favourable; you do not reach Act by trusting the model more, you reach it by making the blast radius small enough that being wrong is cheap and undoable. The gate it requires: no per-action human gate, but hard pre-execution guardrails instead — scoped least-privilege credentials, spend/rate limits, allow-listed tools and MCP servers, input/output validation, and a kill switch — plus comprehensive after-the-fact audit logging and (often) an LLM-as-judge or eval harness scoring a sample of executed actions. The tell: 'it just does it,' 'no human in the loop,' 'too high-volume to approve each one.' Failure mode of granting authority too broadly: scoping Act onto an irreversible or high-cost action because the demo looked reliable — the first compounding error or prompt-injected tool call executes at machine speed with no human between it and production, and you discover the missing gate from the incident, not the design. Also: privilege over-grant (broad credentials turning a small bug into a large breach) and silent drift (no eval harness, so accuracy decays unnoticed). Cost envelope: highest operational and governance cost — full guardrail stack, audit pipeline, continuous evals, and incident-response readiness; cheapest per individual action but most expensive to run safely.
Blast-radius miscalibration: Act is granted on an action that turns out to be irreversible or high-cost, so a single error executes at machine speed with no human able to intervene. Privilege over-grant: broad standing credentials instead of scoped least-privilege tools mean one injected or buggy call can reach far beyond its intended scope. Silent accuracy drift: without continuous LLM-as-judge / eval sampling on executed actions, degradation goes undetected until it surfaces as a production incident.
Act-with-approval tier — flip down the moment any action in scope is irreversible, high-cost-of-error, or where the override rate hasn't been proven low; keep the durable approval gate until the blast radius is genuinely small. Suggest tier — flip all the way down for safety-, legal-, or money-critical actions where no guardrail stack makes unattended execution acceptable; advisory output plus a human trigger is the correct ceiling there.
autonomy-ladder act full-autonomy guardrails least-privilege blast-radius llm-as-judge audit-log kill-switch

docs.title: EU AI Act: Prohibited-practice tier (Article 5) — the redesign-or-kill gate
docs.text:
EU AI Act: Prohibited-practice tier (Article 5) — the redesign-or-kill gate
How a use case lands in the Article 5 unacceptable-risk tier (manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, untargeted facial scraping, workplace/education emotion inference, certain biometric categorisation and real-time public biometric ID), what that bans, and why you screen for it before you architect anything.
Use this when a CTO describes a system that scores or ranks people by behaviour, nudges them subliminally, infers emotion in the workplace or a classroom, scrapes faces to build a recognition database, or does real-time remote biometric identification in public. The tell: the value proposition depends on a capability the Act bans outright — there is no documentation, conformity assessment, or human-in-the-loop that buys it back. This is a kill-or-redesign gate, not a controls problem. Run it as the first node in triage, before high-risk obligations are even loaded, because a prohibited finding short-circuits everything downstream. The design-input point is sharp here: discovering Article 5 exposure in a launch review means the core mechanic is illegal and the build is sunk cost; discovering it in a one-paragraph intake screen costs an afternoon. Most prohibited practices have a lawful adjacent design — one-to-one biometric verification instead of categorisation, fact-based human-assisted risk assessment instead of personality-only profiling — so the output is usually 'rescope and re-triage,' not 'abandon.' Cost envelope: a mis-tier here is the most expensive error in the whole regime — penalties reach the top fine band (low tens of millions of EUR or a mid-single-digit percentage of worldwide turnover) plus forced withdrawal of a shipped product.
Treating a banned mechanic as a 'guardrail problem' — adding human oversight, disclosure, or a reranker to a practice that is prohibited regardless of mitigations, which buys nothing Reasoning from a vague pitch and missing that the marketed feature (e.g. emotion-aware coaching at work) is the exact thing Article 5 names, because the intake text used a euphemism Catching the prohibition only at a pre-launch legal review, after the architecture and data pipeline are built around the illegal capability
Folding prohibited cases into the high-risk checklist and 'over-complying' with Articles 9–15 — rejected because no amount of risk management legalises a banned practice; flip only if a narrow statutory exception genuinely applies (e.g. a tightly-scoped law-enforcement carve-out) and a qualified lawyer signs off Letting the LLM both detect and silently auto-route prohibited cases without a human gate — rejected because a false-negative here is catastrophic; flip never for this tier
eu-ai-act article-5 prohibited unacceptable-risk governance biometric social-scoring compliance-by-design

docs.title: EU AI Act: High-risk tier (Article 6 / Annex III) — the heavy-obligations bucket
docs.text:
EU AI Act: High-risk tier (Article 6 / Annex III) — the heavy-obligations bucket
How a use case lands in the high-risk tier — either as a safety component under Annex I product law, or by falling in an Annex III domain (employment, education, credit/essential services, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration, biometrics) without an Article 6(3) derogation — and the full provider obligation stack it triggers.
Reach for this when the system decides or materially influences something consequential about a person: who gets hired, graded, lent to, admitted, triaged, or policed — or when it is a safety component of a regulated product. The tell is impact on access to rights, livelihood, or safety, in a named Annex III domain. This is the tier that carries the heavy obligation stack: a lifecycle risk-management system (Art 9), data governance on training/validation/test sets (Art 10), technical documentation before market placement (Art 11), automatic event logging (Art 12), transparency and instructions for use (Art 13), effective human oversight with the ability to intervene/override/interrupt (Art 14), accuracy-robustness-cybersecurity (Art 15), conformity assessment and CE marking with EU-database registration, plus deployer duties (Art 26). The Article 6(3) derogation is the live argument: narrow procedural tasks, improving a completed human activity, detecting deviations, or preparatory tasks can drop a system out — but profiling of natural persons always pulls it back in. The design-input point dominates this tier: Articles 12, 14, and 15 are architecture (durable logging, interrupt+checkpointer HITL, eval-backed accuracy thresholds), not paperwork — retrofitting human oversight and traceability into a system that wasn't built for them is a partial rebuild. Cost envelope: months of conformity work and ongoing post-market monitoring; second-band penalties for non-compliance.
Assuming an Annex III domain is automatically high-risk and skipping the Article 6(3) derogation analysis (or the reverse — claiming the derogation while the system profiles people, which voids it) Designing oversight as a post-hoc dashboard rather than a real interrupt point, so 'human oversight' can't actually stop or reverse a decision when Article 14 demands it Building logging and traceability as an afterthought, then being unable to produce the Article 11/12 technical documentation and event history a conformity assessment requires
Self-classifying as limited-risk to dodge the obligation stack — rejected because a wrong downgrade in an Annex III domain is exactly the high-penalty scenario; flip only on a documented Article 6(3) derogation that survives the profiling carve-out Treating the deployer role as obligation-free because 'we only use a vendor system' — rejected because Article 26 imposes real deployer duties; flip never, though the provider/deployer split changes which duties land where
eu-ai-act article-6 annex-iii high-risk conformity-assessment human-oversight ce-marking risk-management governance

docs.title: EU AI Act: Limited-risk tier (Article 50) — transparency duties only
docs.text:
EU AI Act: Limited-risk tier (Article 50) — transparency duties only
How a use case lands in the limited-risk / transparency tier — chatbots and conversational agents, AI-generated or manipulated content, deepfakes, and emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation disclosure — and why the obligations are disclosure-and-labelling, not a conformity regime.
Use this for the large middle of generative and conversational AI: an LLM assistant a user talks to, a system that produces synthetic audio/image/video/text, a deepfake, or a feature that does emotion recognition or biometric categorisation outside the prohibited and high-risk contexts. The tell: the system interacts with or generates content for people, but does not make a consequential Annex III decision about them. The obligations are narrow and concrete — tell people they're interacting with an AI unless it's obvious (Art 50(1)); mark machine-generated content as artificial in a machine-readable way where feasible (Art 50(2)); disclose emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation exposure and handle the data under GDPR (Art 50(3)); clearly label deepfakes (Art 50(4)). No risk-management system, no conformity assessment, no CE marking. The design-input point here is cheap-but-load-bearing: provenance watermarking, content-credential metadata, and an 'AI' disclosure affordance are trivial if designed in at the generation/UI layer and awkward to bolt on after a model and frontend ship. The frequent error is over-classifying — assuming any LLM in the stack is high-risk — which burns months on conformity work the Act doesn't require; the opposite error is forgetting that a limited-risk chatbot wired into a credit or hiring decision inherits the high-risk tier of that decision. Cost envelope: low — disclosure UX plus content labelling, no notified-body involvement.
Over-classifying every generative or conversational feature as high-risk and incurring conformity cost the Act never asked for Under-classifying by ignoring the deployment context — a 'chatbot' that screens job applicants or triages benefits is high-risk via the underlying decision, not limited-risk Treating watermarking/disclosure as a launch-checklist line item, then finding the model and frontend can't emit machine-readable provenance without rework
Skipping disclosure on the grounds that 'users can obviously tell it's a bot' — rejected unless obviousness is genuine and documented; flip only when the AI nature is unmistakable from context (Art 50(1)'s own exception) Bundling limited-risk transparency into a single generic 'AI policy' page instead of in-context labelling — rejected because Article 50 wants disclosure at the point of interaction/content; flip only where a regulator-accepted equivalent surfaces the same information
eu-ai-act article-50 limited-risk transparency deepfake watermarking chatbot-disclosure provenance governance

docs.title: EU AI Act: Minimal-risk tier — no specific obligations, but re-triage on drift
docs.text:
EU AI Act: Minimal-risk tier — no specific obligations, but re-triage on drift
How a use case lands in the minimal-risk tier (everything outside Articles 5, 6/Annex III, and 50 — spam filters, recommendation/ranking, internal analytics, most back-office ML), what still applies (GDPR, sector law, voluntary codes), and why a minimal classification is a fact about today's design, not a permanent grant.
Use this as the default landing zone: spam and fraud filters, search ranking and recommendation, demand forecasting, internal copilots over non-personal data, most back-office and product-analytics ML. The tell: no banned mechanic, no consequential Annex III decision about a person, no human-facing interaction or synthetic-content generation that triggers Article 50. The Act imposes no specific obligations here — but 'minimal under the AI Act' is not 'unregulated.' GDPR still governs any personal data, consumer-protection and sector rules still bind, and the EU encourages voluntary codes of conduct; adopting transparency, logging, or oversight practices ahead of need is cheap insurance against scope drift. The design-input point is about durability of the classification, not heavy controls: minimal is a snapshot of the current intended purpose, and the cheapest governance move is to wire a re-triage trigger to any material change — a new data source, a new audience, a feature that starts influencing a hiring/credit/safety decision, or profiling creeping in. A system that was minimal can silently become high-risk or limited-risk the day its purpose shifts, and the failure is discovering that in an audit rather than at the design change. Cost envelope: effectively zero AI-Act-specific cost; the only spend is the discipline of re-classifying when the use case moves.
Treating a minimal classification as permanent and skipping re-triage when the system's purpose, data, or audience changes — silent drift into high-risk or limited-risk Reading 'minimal risk under the AI Act' as 'no compliance at all' and neglecting GDPR, sector law, or consumer-protection duties that still apply Letting profiling or a consequential decision creep into a back-office model without anyone re-running the tier check, voiding the original minimal finding
Applying high-risk-style controls 'to be safe' across all minimal systems — rejected as governance theatre that burns budget and slows shipping; flip only where a voluntary code or a near-term roadmap change makes pre-investment in oversight genuinely cheaper than retrofitting Classifying once at launch and never revisiting — rejected because tier is a function of intended purpose, which mutates; flip never, the re-triage trigger is the whole point of this tier
eu-ai-act minimal-risk scope-drift re-triage gdpr voluntary-codes recommendation back-office-ml governance
